forum.title: U5 DMA not setting interrupt or executing callback, stays busy
forum.best_answer_content:
I’ve possibly found the cause.  It’s related to GNU tools 14.3.rel1.  I’m going to file a bug report on it.  It’s solved by going back to 13.3.rel1.

Details there.  PS: FreeRTOS forum was of no help.

forum.author: Harvey White

scraped_replies.html:
Hi Harvey,

First DMA transfer OK, then SPI stuck at HAL_BUSY with no interrupt/callback usually means the GPDMA channel completion IRQ never reaches the HAL, so the SPI state never returns to READY and the next call fails. A few things to check:

1.Is the channel IRQ enabled and routed? 

HAL_NVIC_EnableIRQ(GPDMA1_Channel0_IRQn); in your MSP init
In stm32u5xx_it.c: GPDMA1_Channel0_IRQHandler() calling HAL_DMA_IRQHandler(&handle_GPDMA1_Channel0);
To test it, put a breakpoint in the channel IRQ handler and in HAL_SPI_TxCpltCallback(). If neither hits, that's it.

 

2. Is DMA linked to the TX handle? __HAL_LINKDMA(&hspi1, hdmatx, handle_GPDMA1_Channel0);

3. Channel params for memory→peripheral? Direction = DMA_MEMORY_TO_PERIPH, Request = GPDMA1_REQUEST_SPI1_TX, memory increment on / peripheral increment off, data widths matching your frame size.

 

Could you share your MX_GPDMA1_Init/channel config, the relevant stm32u5xx_it.c, and how you're polling? 

 

Kind regards, 

DHIF Khaled

scraped_replies.author: Harvey White

scraped_replies.html:
Thanks ​@Harvey White ,

The timers working while SPI, DMA and DMA2D stay quiet feels like the useful clue, when a whole group of interrupts is silent even with the NVIC enable in place, it usually points to something above the individual peripherals rather than a per-peripheral mistake.

A couple of things that might be worth a look:

  • One is whether the interrupts are being masked. It could be worth checking if BASEPRI or PRIMASK is non-zero around the point you'd expect the IRQ. A lingering critical section could hold off your priority-5 interrupts while a higher-priority timer still slips through. I noticed some RTOS bits (`RTOS_ILI9341`, `taskENTER_CRITICAL`), are you running an RTOS? If so, running the transfer before the scheduler starts might tell you a lot.
  • The other, since it's a U5, is TrustZone. If it's enabled, it might be worth confirming SPI1/GPDMA1/DMA2D aren't landing on the secure side (GTZC / NVIC `ITNS`) while your code runs non-secure the ISR would vector to the other state and never reach you. Timers being non-secure could explain the difference.
  • One more thing: `HAL_SPI_Transmit_DMA()` and `HAL_DMA_PollForTransfer()` may be working against each other, since the poll clears the TC flag itself, that could be why the callback never runs and `hspi1.State` doesn't return to `READY`, which lines up with the `HAL_BUSY` you're seeing.

Would you be able to say whether you're running an RTOS and whether TrustZone is enabled? That'd help narrow it down.

Kind regards,
DHIF Khaled

scraped_replies.html:
Further information, a solution without explanation.

I have started rewriting the native FreeRTOS calls into CMSIS_OS2 calls.  This seems to work.  I suspect that there might be something either odd or possibly corrupted in the FreeRTOS calls,  So, problem “solved” 

Now, the entire DMA problem can be reworked (as in one display line written, but no others).

note the following:

  1. The routine that is doing the transfer setups is in C++, the interrupt routines are in C.
  2. Create a callback, use SPI Tx complete. 
    1. There are two possibilities to monitor on a DMA driven SPI transfer.  The DMA is likely called once per SPI reload.  Monitoring the DMA itself is not useful.  The SPI transfer is the entire block needed to transfer, and this provides the desired information.
    2. the relevant it.c routines do not need to be modified.  They provide no useful information.  What you can profitably use is the HAL_SPI_TxCpltCallback.  This is not called on each SPI transfer, but only when the block is completely sent (which you want).
    3. I put the callback i a separate C routine.  Note that the tag variable is declared volatile, which forces the system to read the variable each time, rather than cache it somewhere in a register.
  3. See the code fragments to see the methods.

 

volatile bool ILI9341_tag;

// if this is omitted, DMA does not work

#ifdef _ILI9341_DMA // DISPLAY INTERFACE MODE

void HAL_SPI_TxCpltCallback(SPI_HandleTypeDef *hspi1)

{ILI9341_tag = true;

}

#endif

 

// if this is omitted, IRQ does not work

#ifdef _ILI9341_IRQ // DISPLAY INTERFACE MODE

void HAL_SPI_TxCpltCallback(SPI_HandleTypeDef *hspi1)

{ILI9341_tag = true;

}#endif

 

This is placed in the C callbacks routine.

 

#if (defined _ILI9341_DMA)

// DMA CALLBACK RELEASES SEMAPHORE

ILI9341_tag = false;

result = HAL_SPI_Transmit_DMA(SPI_interface, (unsigned char*)&QVGA_image.Ppixel[y][rect.x0],2*(dx+1)); // 2 bytes/pixel

while (ILI9341_tag == false); // osDelay(1);

ILI9341_tag = false;

 

#elif (defined _ILI9341_IRQ)

// This can be either 1 D or 2 D,

ILI9341_tag = false;

// CALLBACK RELEASES SEMAPHORE

result = HAL_SPI_Transmit_IT(SPI_interface, (unsigned char*)&QVGA_image.Ppixel[y][rect.x0],2*(dx+1)); // 2 bytes/pixel

while (ILI9341_tag == false);

ILI9341_tag = false;

#else

// if translate is true, then RGB565 is called, and QVGA_image is the source

// if translate is false, then RGB565 is not called, and QVGA_image is the source

result = HAL_SPI_Transmit(SPI_interface, (unsigned char*)&QVGA_image.Ppixel[y][rect.x0],2*(dx+1), 150); // 2 bytes/pixel

#ifdef _ERROR1

if (result != HAL_OK) ERROR1(__FILE__, __LINE__, (char*)"ILI9341 DATA ERROR");

#endif

#endif

 

Note that this allows the driver to be run in either blocking mode, IRQ mode, or DMA mode.  The relevant IRQ must be enabled in CubeMX.  

Note also that the callback uses the default callback label, and does not require registering since it’s a weak binding to that routine name.

As a practical note:

The DMA driver is faster than the IRQ driver which is faster than the blocking driver.  This is expected.  Note that the driver is used in a blocking mode, since the display needs to have exclusive access. 

The overall procedure is to write to a virtual display of 32 bit color, then upon request, translate to a 16 bit RGB565 buffer, and then transfer that to the display. 

At some point, the limiting factor in the transfer is the size of the transfer and the speed of the SPI interface.  That interface speed is limited by the maximum clock speed of the display driver chip.
